data.title: Bojnice – a Slavic hillfort and a centre of tar production
data.excerpt: Bojnice is known for the prehistoric occupation of the Prepoštská Cave and for the fairy-tale neo-Gothic castle rebuilt into its present form by Ján Pálffy. Archaeology has added a third story: an extensive Slavic occupation on the loam terraces of the river Nitra, with nine semi-sunken dwellings and batteries of tar pits unique of their kind in Slovakia.
data.metaTitle: Bojnice – Slavic hillfort and centre of tar production
data.metaDescription: Besides its castle and the Prepoštská Cave, Bojnice also hides a major Slavic occupation and traces of tar production on the terraces of the Nitra.

keyFacts.label: Extent of the occupation
keyFacts.value: Slavic settlement and production features covered c. 200 ha on the slopes of the loam terrace of the Nitra, divided by the Kaňanka, Jarok and Dubnička streams

keyFacts.label: Semi-sunken dwellings discovered
keyFacts.value: Nine badly damaged single-roomed semi-sunken buildings measuring c. 3 × 4 m at the locality of Dolné lány, with further dwellings at Lipiny and below the hospital

keyFacts.label: Unique tar pits
keyFacts.value: A battery of four tar pits c. 110–140 cm in diameter at the locality of Zadné lány ranks among the features unique of their kind in Slovakia

keyFacts.label: Distance between the find spots
keyFacts.value: The tar-pit find spots of Zadné lány and Vrábecké are about 950 m apart as the crow flies

keyFacts.label: Origin of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: The hillfort on the castle knoll was probably built already by the people of the Púchov culture and later adapted by the Slavs

keyFacts.label: The tar-making process
keyFacts.value: Dry distillation of wood took place inside the pits, gradually producing tar and charcoal at temperatures of roughly 120–500 °C

keyFacts.label: The many uses of tar
keyFacts.value: Tar was used in cooperage, wheelwrighting, tanning, rope-making, for military purposes and in fruit growing, and charcoal in turn in smithies

keyFacts.label: Evidence of long-distance trade
keyFacts.value: Trade in tar in the upper Nitra region is documented by finds of iron axe-shaped currency bars at Bošany, Žabokreky and Bojná

children.text: Bojnice is known not only for the prehistoric occupation of the Prepoštská Cave
http://muzeumpraveku.sk/

and for the fairy-tale neo-Gothic castle that Ján Pálffy had rebuilt into its present form, but also for a significant Slavic occupation found not only in the area of today’s castle but also in its surroundings.

Slavic settlement and production features lay on the slopes of a massive loam terrace of the Nitra, divided by the tributaries Kaňanka, Jarok and Dubnička into several distinct localities, each with its own name (Nemocnica, Predné lány, Dolné lány, Zadné lány, Lipiny, Vrábecké). This whole area covers c. 200 ha, and in the 1960s dark patches were discovered on it, distributed fairly regularly across the north-eastern slope of the Dolné lány locality. Excavation showed that these were nine badly damaged single-roomed semi-sunken buildings (measuring c. 3 × 4 m), typical of settlements of this character throughout Slavic territory. Further dwellings were identified at Lipiny and later two more on the slope below the hospital.

blocks.caption: The Prepoštská Cave – home of the Neanderthal
blocks.alt: The Prepoštská Cave – home of the Neanderthal

children.text: The distant ancestors from Bojnice, as we know from other Slavic sites too, built their houses – semi-sunken buildings – by sinking part of them into the ground and leaving part raised above it. This above-ground part had wattle walls daubed with clay, so-called daub, which was found in the fill of all the features. The roofing of a semi-sunken building depended on the load-bearing post construction. Most probably it was a gabled roof. The floor of the dwellings was of trodden clay and a hearth built of stones was usually placed in the corner. Similar dwellings of an unfortified settlement of the 9th–10th centuries in south-western Slovakia are known at Nitriansky Hrádok.

The Bojnice huts are characterised by an abundance of iron slag and clinker, which are produced when iron is worked. In the fill of the features sherds of Slavic pottery were come upon, already made on the potter’s wheel and decorated with the typical wavy line, impressions, horizontal lines or incisions arranged into a chevron pattern and other variations. The vessels were made of clay mixed with finer or coarser sand and sometimes with mica. Besides pottery, the features yielded small iron knives, an arrowhead, animal bones, a clay crucible and also a clay tuyère used to blow air during iron smelting. The finds document the existence of iron-smelting and smithing workshops of the 9th–10th centuries. Tar kilns were also found in the vicinity of the settlements.
The hillfort

blocks.alt: Bojnice – a Slavic hillfort and a centre of tar production

children.text: The hillfort on the castle knoll was probably built already by the people of the Púchov culture, and the Slavs later adapted it to their own needs. Later repeated rebuildings of the castle and its grounds destroyed most of the traces of the Slavic hillfort in the area of today’s Bojnice castle. Nevertheless, archaeology has managed to prove the existence of a Slavic hillfort in this area. In the later period of the building of the Hungarian state the hillfort continued to be used, and the very first written mention of Bojnice, in the charter of Zobor Abbey of 1113, refers to the suburbium of Bojnice, „de suburbanis Baimoz…“, which made the hillfort the oldest historically documented built monument of Bojnice. The fortified hillfort stood in 1113 and at some later time – probably during the feverish building of stone castles after the devastating Mongol invasion of 1241–1242 – it was rebuilt into a stone castle, of which there are records from 1302. It was also a centre of religious life, because church administration settled at the royal castles and castle parishes were created. The Zobor charter of 1113 already mentions a parish, but the church is not mentioned until 1244. The charter also records healing springs.
Bojnice was probably home to renowned tar burners

The most remarkable and at the same time the most important discovery at Bojnice are the tar pits at the localities of Zadné lány and Vrábecké. The two sites are about 950 m apart as the crow flies. They are undoubtedly features unique of their kind in Slovakia.

A battery of four tar pits was discovered at Zadné lány when the tractor driver Galanský, ploughing on the south-eastern slope at the point which rises highest above the deep cutting of a field track, struck the hard-fired upper parts of the pits with his plough, tore them away and scattered them in the immediate vicinity. After the surface had been cleaned, four regular circles c. 110–140 cm in diameter appeared, with an undisturbed dark ring burnt around the circumference. All the pits were built in the same way: one half of the floor remained firm and undisturbed, while in the other half the clay was dug out further until a lower-lying hollow of the desired dimensions was created, partly undercutting the firm floor. The tar flowing out collected in this hollow. The fill of the pits at Zadné lány contained pieces of charred wood, probably pine or spruce, and ash-coloured clay. Closer to the bottom, lumps of a light, pitch-black porous substance began to appear sporadically, which gave off a characteristic smell when heated. In the first pit a few typical Slavic sherds and several charred grains of pulses were found. From the second pit come vessel rims and two incomplete bases with relief marks.

children.text: Almost simultaneously with the discovery of the pits at Zadné lány, another find spot of tar-production features was come upon at the locality of Vrábecké. These pits showed certain differences in the construction and internal arrangement of the features. In the upper part of one pit lay a damaged vessel with a wide mouth and an everted rim, made of a coarse sandy material which turned brick-red on contact with high temperature. In shape and size it corresponds exactly to the dimensions of the hollow into which it was placed to collect the tar. The asymmetrically coarse appearance of the vessel is due to its being handmade. More pronounced traces of wheel-finishing are discernible only in the upper third. A considerably thick coating of tar was preserved inside the vessel. In both cases the tar pits consist of the chamber proper, into which the raw material was loaded, and a lower hollow where the tar collected. The pits at Zadné lány contained pieces of charred wood, whereas the features at Vrábecké were filled to the brim with tree bark. The situation at Zadné lány thus indicates that the whole battery was abandoned after its contents had been removed, while the charred tree bark in the pits at the site of Vrábecké suggests that the features were abandoned in the course of production. The pits at Zadné lány, and likewise those at Vrábecké, were put into production all at once. It remains unclear, however, whether the features at the two localities can be regarded as entirely contemporary, or whether the differences in internal arrangement are an expression of a chronological sequence corresponding to the removal of the whole settlement to the neighbouring locality, where new production workshops and dwellings were established.

The discovery of the tar pits at Bojnice is an invitation to take a closer look at this important specialised craft in this country in the Slavic period. Producers of pitch are already mentioned in Czech sources of the 11th century under the name pkelník-picarius. Somewhat later, Hungarian sources record a distinct servile class under the term bucharii-pohárnici, perhaps also engaged in the production of pitch. In Slovakia the existence of tar production as a specialised craft as early as the time of Great Moravia was until recently documented only by linguistic and historical research, and in particular by toponymy. In the 1960s R. Krajčovič, on the basis of an analysis of place names and their comparison with the archaeological material, concluded that the occupational names of villages in Slovakia (preserved in later centuries too, or down to the present day) belong to the oldest group, which came into being in the 8th and 9th centuries. Dechtice and Smolenice are names of this kind; their inhabitants were engaged in the production of tar and pitch. Historians have arrived at similar insights.

children.text: Tar, produced on an extended scale (batteries of tar pits), satisfied not only the demands of local consumption but became an object of trade with nearer and more distant regions, which in the upper Nitra region is undoubtedly documented by finds of iron axe-shaped currency bars at Bošany, Žabokreky and Bojná. The tradition of Great Moravian tar production in the Prievidza area survived practically until recently. In the 1960s some local people still vividly remembered tar kilns on the neighbouring hills in the cadastral area of Dubnica. Vanished tar works in nearby Jalovec are likewise remembered.
What was tar used for?

The production of tar in this period satisfied not only local consumption; tar was also intended for trade. It was used in cooperage, wheelwrighting, tanning, rope-making, for military purposes and in fruit growing. Charcoal, as a by-product, was used in the smithies discovered at Bojnice and Brezany. The tradition of Great Moravian tar production survived into the 1950s, when some inhabitants still vividly remembered tar kilns on the hills in the cadastral area of Dubnica.
How did the Slavs make tar?

blocks.alt: Bojnice – a Slavic hillfort and a centre of tar production

children.text:
The actual process of producing tar in these pits was preceded by preparatory work. A small container was placed in the hollow, and above it, at the level of the firm floor, a partition was set, probably of wood and of such dimensions and shape as the mouth of the cavity. The partition rested on a step-like projection in the wall of the pit and with its straight edge sat in turn on a board projecting from the firm floor. This gave half of the floor a slope towards the centre. The surface of the partition had to be protected from the fire by a layer of clay. A deposit of tar at the edge of the firm floor indicates that a gap remained between the firm floor and the partition in the upper part, through which the tar ran down onto a suitably adapted board of the firm floor and from there into the container. Logs were loaded onto the floor prepared in this way right up to the brim, and after the wood had been set alight the mouth of the pit was closed and covered over with clay. Dry distillation took place inside, producing charcoal, tar and other combustion products. It is known that at 120–150 °C wood dries out and loses water, then at around 150–270 °C thermolysis with chemical changes sets in, culminating at about 275–450 °C in the formation and evaporation of liquid products. At 450–500 °C the remaining substances are carbonised and charcoal is formed. Throughout the process of dry distillation various compounds are produced, among them tar and charcoal. The principles of making both charcoal and wood tar have essentially not changed since the beginning of the Bronze Age. Only the working procedure and the productivity of production differ in the following periods.
 
 You can see the procedure for making tar in the Slavic period on this excellent website:

children.text: The production settlement and tar works at Bojnice, which came into being and operated above all in the Great Moravian period but may have survived on this spot into the 10th century, point to the proximity of some larger central hillfort, around which settlements of various functions were spread. In the light of these discoveries the Bojnice–Prievidza area appears as another important centre of the Great Moravian and post-Great Moravian periods, which in the process of the separation of crafts from agriculture reached a high level of specialised crafts, concentrated not directly at the hillfort but in unfortified – and perhaps sometimes fortified – settlements in the immediate vicinity.
